explanation: A string is written in single quotes, and its text is exactly what is written between them: there are no escapes and no interpolation, so braces, backslashes and double quotes are ordinary characters. `'{x}'` is the three characters `{x}`, and `'a\nb'` keeps its backslash.

source:
Greeting('en') = 'Hello'
Greeting('lv') = 'Sveiki'
Greeting(x) = '?'

Greeting('lv')
Greeting('de')
Greeting(5)
explanation: A string in a clause head is a literal pattern: the clause is selected only for exactly that text. Any other value, a different string or a number, falls through to a later clause.

A string is a value like any other: it can stand beside numbers in a sequence or a list, and each item keeps its own kind. Nothing turns a number into text or joins items into one string, so a number beside a string is still a number, and `+` on strings is a type error.
KatLang has one string literal form, single quotes. A double quote outside a single-quoted string or a comment is an error: write `'Hello'`.
